newsitem.title: MADAGASCAR: Madagascar's former ruler completes comeback.
newsitem.headline: Madagascar's former ruler completes comeback.

text.p: Madagascar's former military ruler Didier Ratsiraka made a dramatic comeback on Friday when he was declared president four years after the islanders drummed him out of office.
The High Constitutional Court declared the 60-year-old retired admiral the winner of last year's elections by the narrowest of margins.
Ending weeks of suspense, the court said Ratsiraka won 50.7 percent of the vote against 49.3 percent for Albert Zafy, the medical professor who trounced him in 1993.
"I will do my utmost to defeat poverty and ensure that the Malagasy people have a decent standard of living," Ratsiraka said at a ceremony proclaiming him president for the next five years.

The army warned on Thursday it would not tolerate violence by supporters of the beaten candidate. It moved armoured cars onto the streets of the capital Antananarivo late on Thursday but the city was calm after Friday's proclamation.
At the ceremony a minute's silence was observed for victims of Cyclone Gretelle that hit southern Madagascar last weekend. At least 50 people were killed and thousands made homeless.
"I shall do all I can to alleviate the suffering of the inhabitants of the region," Ratsiraka said.

Ratsiraka's was the second comeback by a former African strongman ousted by the pro-democracy movement which swept the continent from 1989 to 1992. Benin's Mathieu Kerekou was voted back as president last year.

Ratsiraka went into voluntary exile in France after he was beaten by Zafy in 1993 in a vote that ended two years of violent protests for democracy. Ratsiraka had ruled since 1975 and for most of that time was a convinced Marxist whose policies wrecked the economy of the world's fourth-largest island.

Zafy took over but Madagascar's dreams of a new future quickly evaporated because of infighting between the new politicians in charge. The 14 million islanders remain among the poorest people on earth.

The early elections were ordered after 69-year-old Zafy was impeached by parliament last year for repeated violations of the constitution. He and Ratsiraka topped a first round of voting last November 3 between 15 candidates and then went into a head-to-head contest on December 29.
Release of provisional results was suspended early this month after most had been broadcast because Zafy complained the figures were being manipulated in favour of Ratsiraka.
The warning by the armed forces, gendarmerie and police on Thursday followed persistent rumours that supporters of the losing candidate would provoke unrest.

"The forces of order will not hesitate to apply with firmness all necessary measures to block all subversive activities...to maintain and if necessary re-establish public order," they said in a statement.
Madagascar has had an interim president, Norbert Ratsirahonana, since Zafy's impeachment and during the elections.
Ratsiraka campaigned on promises of establishing a "humanistic and ecological republic" in Madagascar.
He said on Friday one of his first goals was to revise the constitution, submitting to a referendum two options: keeping a unitary state or installing a federal system.
